opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. My honest answer is that, in research at least, nobody hands you the problem. There's no committee that sits down and says, "These are the ten problems the world needs solved." Problems get defined by people who are close enough to reality to feel that something is wrong, or missing, and who are stubborn enough to articulate it clearly.

In AI, people often assume that industry, the big labs with all the compute, now define the problems, and in many ways they do set the agenda: scaling, products, benchmarks everyone chases. But I think that's a bit of an illusion. A lot of what industry is scaling today started as a weird, unfashionable question someone in a lab asked years earlier. Representation learning, self-supervision, how vision and language should relate: these weren't obvious priorities until someone insisted they were.

So I'd say problems are defined by taste. It's the researcher's job, maybe the most important part of it, to decide what's worth working on before it's obvious. Solving a well-posed problem is, in some sense, the easier part. Look at visual intelligence, for example. Language models have gotten incredibly good, but I don't think we've really figured out what it means for a machine to see and understand the physical world. Defining that properly, beyond "get a higher number on this dataset," is itself the open problem.

And I think that's also why academia still matters. Not because it can compete on scale, but because it has the freedom to ask questions that don't have an immediate payoff. If everyone only works on the problems that are already defined, we end up optimizing the same things more and more efficiently, and we stop discovering what we should have been optimizing in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says problems are defined by people close enough to reality to notice what is wrong or missing, which conveys that people who experience the world define them.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because in research the hardest part is usually not solving the problem, it's figuring out which problem is worth solving.

I'd say nobody defines it alone. There's this romantic idea that a single genius sits down and decides what matters, but that's almost never how it works. Problems get defined by a kind of ecosystem. Part of it is the community, the collective taste of the field. Part of it is the tools and data you happen to have at a given moment, which quietly shape what even looks like a tractable question. And part of it is just the real world pushing back on you, telling you that something you built doesn't work the way you hoped.

For me personally, a lot of the problems I've worked on came from a sense of discomfort. You look at how things are being done and something feels unnecessarily complicated, or a story people are telling doesn't quite line up with the evidence. With ConvNeXt, for example, the question wasn't "how do we beat transformers," it was more "wait, do we actually understand why transformers are winning, or are we just attributing it to the wrong thing?" That irritation, that feeling of "this explanation is too easy," is often where a good problem comes from.

But I also want to be honest that in the current moment, a lot of problem definition is being driven from outside academia. The big labs, the scale of compute, the commercial incentives, these set the agenda whether we like it or not. And I think the role of people in a position like mine, in a university, is partly to resist that a little. Not to ignore what industry is doing, but to ask the questions that don't get asked when everything is optimized for the next product release. Things like, what are these models actually learning about the visual world? Do they have anything resembling a world model, or are they just very good at pattern completion? Those are problems that no one is forced to define, so someone has to choose to.

So if you pressed me, I'd say the people who define problems are the people with the courage to be confused in public. The ones who are willing to say "I don't think we understand this," when everyone else is moving on. That's not a title or an institution, it's more of a disposition. And I think the field is healthiest when that disposition is spread across many people, not concentrated in a few.

r001.rationale: The response says problems are defined by an ecosystem, including the research community, available tools and data, and outside forces such as big labs and commercial incentives. It does not identify the people who inhabit the world as the ones defining problems.

astra-6.text:
I think anyone can define a problem, but whether it’s a problem worth solving is a much harder question. In research, we often inherit problems from the community. There’s a benchmark, there’s a metric, and everyone works on improving it. That gives us a shared direction, but it’s easy to forget to ask why that direction matters.

To me, defining a good problem comes from connecting what you understand technically with something that’s missing in practice. Sometimes researchers see that gap; sometimes the people using the technology see it much more clearly. So I don’t think any one group gets to decide. You need that interaction—and you need the willingness to question the problems everyone else has already accepted.

r001.rationale: The response says “anyone can define a problem” and adds that researchers and people using technology both identify gaps, communicating that people generally define problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think anyone can define a problem. The harder question is whether it’s a problem worth solving, and worth solving for whom. As researchers, we often inherit problems from our community. There’s a benchmark, there’s a metric, and we start trying to improve it. But choosing the metric already reflects somebody’s judgment about what matters.

So I don’t think that authority belongs exclusively to researchers, companies, or governments. People experiencing a problem should have a voice in defining it. Our responsibility is to listen, question our assumptions, and connect what we’re capable of doing with what people actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says anyone can define a problem and specifically says people experiencing it should have a voice in defining it.
